rv.q: A show this steeped in grief and heartbreak has never felt so damn good.

To the great credit of everyone involved, “The Notebook” also delivers unexpectedly sophisticated theatricality with the requisite supercharging of the tear ducts, notwithstanding an archly familiar narrative.
The Notebook is a musical that knows exactly what it is: a big, swoony, unabashedly romantic spectacle that trades in the currency of feelings.
But its creators, including singer-songwriter Ingrid Michaelson and “This Is Us” writer and producer Bekah Brunstetter, target feeling at the expense of character, specificity or surprise.

Because as elegantly staged as “The Notebook” is by co-directors Michael Greif and Schele Williams, and despite boasting an appealing cast, the show amounts to a series of un-involving pencil sketches rather than a layered portrait of a decades-long love.
For others, its cloying nature may prove too much.
Plunkett's truthfulness pierces through the sentimentality, and there's something elemental in the combination of love and loss that this pair embodies.

For all its sweetness and polish “The Notebook” never rises to truly transporting heights—except when Ms. Plunkett, as the heroine, Allie, in her later years, and Dorian Harewood, as her husband, Noah, are the focus.
But without leading characters, story or songs that are elevated, this love story remains not only leaden but as slight as jottings in journal.
Or maybe, seen with a cold eye, meretricious.
It is intent now on making a live audience openly weep by employing massive doses of schlocky sentimentality without the aid of Ryan Gosling.
Families who have learned the hard way that Alzheimer’s doesn’t play miracle games have every right to take offense at this baloney.

With its stunning performances, beautiful songs, and supreme stage directing, the musical succeeds in delivering a fresh spin on its original material while also making sure that Noah and Allie’s story is never truly forgotten.
The Notebook works because everyone works together to make the magic happen.
I’m afraid I joined her only in being unimpressed.
Her sensitive portrayal becomes the planet around which everything else revolves.
This could be anyone’s story, and the poetic end that comes for Noah and Allie represents the very happiest resolution.

A shrug from a tear-stained shoulder is certainly not the worst way to exit a musical, so even if The Notebook isn’t reinventing any wheels, it turns them with earnest, somehow not-too-sentimental, precision.
The story is cleverly adapted by librettist Bekah Brunstetter, who seems almost as much guided by the TV series “This Is Us” (where she worked as a writer and producer) as by Sparks’ novel.
The musical version of The Notebook is pleasant enough and its sentiment quotient is kept low until the end when audible sobbing can be heard in the theater.
Woods gives The Notebook the kick in the pants it sorely needs and the dramatic momentum it otherwise seldom earns.
Even with all that first class talent, The Notebook could have done more to earn the love.

But with Hell’s Kitchen, Suffs, Water for Elephants, The Outsiders, Cabaret, Lempicka, The Great Gatsby and more lapping at the gate, or at least the ticket wicket, this three-generation Kleenex-clutching weepie might get lost in the awards season rush.
This compelling conceit gets weakened by a flat book and lyrics.
When these two veteran actors are on stage together, “The Notebook” is the moving, unabashed, heartfelt tearjerker it’s needs to be.
It was thoroughly enjoyable to see a production that swept me up into the gestalt of the world of the show so completely.
This may not be the best musical of the season but it is enjoyable with some unique staging and inventive casting.

cn.t: Critics find this Nicholas Sparks adaptation emotionally manipulative yet effective, with strong performances elevating a schmaltzy, cliché-laden score. Fans of the book and film will likely weep; others may find it too saccharine to embrace.

sg.ra: Shubert/SeatPlan place rows C-E as 'just right' — close enough to catch facial detail without the stage-height skew that rows AA/A suffer inside this shallow 26'9" proscenium house; TickPick singles out row B (seats 105-110) as the best seat in the Schoenfeld.

SeatPlan notes the mezzanine overhang starts at row J but only begins clipping the top of the stage at row Q — so K-P sits in the narrow band that's still unobstructed yet priced below premium; TickPick and Headout independently flag K-P as the value pocket in this 1,079-seat Shubert house.

sg.vl: Overhang cuts the top of the stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly says rows beyond Q lose the top of the stage to the mezzanine overhang, and Headout/TickPick corroborate that under-overhang seats 'might have obstructed views from the overhang of the box seats or the mezzanine itself' — a real issue in this shallow Shubert house where the mezz projects forward.

sg.vl: Overhead sweep of the whole stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both cite front center mezz rows A-B as offering 'excellent overhead views perfect for appreciating the stage in one sweep' — the Schoenfeld's mezz hangs closer to the stage than larger Shubert houses, so row A feels surprisingly close rather than distant.

SeatPlan flags E-G as benefiting from 'great rake for aerial views which cover the entire stage below' — the Schoenfeld mezz is steeper than most Shubert houses, so E-G keeps the full stage visible where a flatter rake would start clipping; Headout calls it a value tier below the premium A-D band.

Multiple sources describe rear mezz past row F as 'a gamble... actors start to look like LEGO figures' — despite the Schoenfeld only having 392 mezz seats, the steep rake trades sightline for proximity and you lose emotional read on faces; a J104 reviewer conceded 'nearly center, no obstructions' but 2nd-to-last row.

SeatPlan notes 'single-digit seats in rows A-D' of the side mezz 'are more directly above the stage and feel surprisingly close' — the Schoenfeld's narrow 40-foot proscenium means side-mezz angles are less punishing than wider houses, though TickPick warns the far edges of rows 'have slightly blocked views of the corners of the stage'.
